UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                   BEFORE THE
                     FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION

Northern Indiana Public Service                                )
Company LLC                                                    )
                                                               )       Docket No. EL26-36-000
v.                                                             )
                                                               )
Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc.                 )


                           REQUEST FOR REHEARING OF
                  THE OFFICE OF THE ILLINOIS ATTORNEY GENERAL

        Pursuant to Rule 713 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal Energy

Regulatory Commission (“Commission” or “FERC”), 18 C.F.R. § 385.713, and Section 313 of the

Federal Power Act (“FPA”), 16 U.S.C. § 825l(a), the People of the State of Illinois, by its Attorney

General, Kwame Raoul (the "People" or “IL OAG”), respectfully submit this Request for

Rehearing of the Commission’s March 19 Order in the above-captioned docket. The IL OAG filed

an intervention in this proceeding and filed comments on January 20, 2026. 1

I.      INTRODUCTION

        On December 23, 2025, the DOE issued the Schahfer Order (202-25-12) 2 to MISO and

Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC (“NIPSCO” or the “Company”), pursuant to

section 202(c) of the Federal Power Act. 3 The DOE Order directs MISO, in coordination with

NIPSCO to ensure that NIPSCO’s R.M. Schahfer Generating Station Units 17 and 18 (“Impacted

Schahfer Units”) remain available for operation during the period of the DOE Order (December

23, 2025, through March 23, 2026). The DOE Order is being challenged by multiple parties outside



1
  Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. EL26-36-
000, Motion to Intervene and Comments of the Office of the Illinois Attorney General (filed January 20, 2026).
2
  U.S. Department of Energy, Order No. 202-25-12 (December 23, 2025) (“DOE Order”).
3
  See 16 U.S.C. § 824(a)(c)

                                                      1
 of FERC in the United States Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. The IL OAG notes that the

DOE Order exceeds DOE’s authority and is not supported by substantial evidence, and the validity

of the DOE Order affects the Commission’s authority to impose costs on Illinois consumers.

        NIPSCO filed a complaint in this proceeding seeking a mechanism for the Company to

obtain rate recovery under FPA Section 202(c) for the costs of operating the Impacted Schahfer

Units, which were scheduled to retire on December 31, 2025. 4 NIPSCO essentially requested the

same recovery mechanism that was approved by FERC for Consumers Energy Company for

operation of the J.H Campbell Generating Plant (“Campbell Plant”). 5 That is allocation via “load

ratio share” of all costs for the continued operation of the Impacted Schahfer Units across MISO

North and Central. The Commission accepted this in its March 19 Order. 6

        The Commission noted that “Parties also may take appropriate steps, such as requesting

rehearing in this proceeding, to preserve arguments that, if the DOE Order were to be modified,

then the Commission should require refunds or otherwise revisit its approach to matters in

connection with the DOE Order.” 7 The costs of running the Impacted Schahfer Units allocated

throughout MISO north/central will be expensive, given that these units were slated to retire. There

will likely be major repair costs as well, especially for Unit 18. Should the DOE Order be vacated,

which the IL OAG has requested of the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, 8 the Commission’s March

19 Order would be without a legal basis. The Commission would then need to create a method for

refunding ratepayers the costs of these expensive units.



4
  Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. EL26-36-
000, Complaint (filed December 29. 2025).
5
  Consumers Energy Co. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 192 FERC ¶ 61,158 (2025) (“Consumers Energy
Order”), order on reh’g, 193 FERC ¶ 61,228 (2025) (“Consumers Energy Rehearing Order”).
6
  Northern Indiana Public Service Company LLC. v. Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 194 FERC ¶ 61,215
(2026) (“March 19 Order”).
7
  March 19 Order at 16-17 (para. 40).
8
  See Sierra Club et. al v. U.S. Dept. of Energy (D.C. Cir. Case No. 26-1056 (consol. with 26-1075 and 26-1077)).

                                                       2
 II.        REQUEST FOR REHEARING

           A. Statement of Issues

       1. In its March 19 Order, the Commission erred in accepting the proposed cost-allocation
method, because it is not supported by substantial evidence in the record, ignores the obligations
of NIPSCO’s customers to pay NIPSCO rates for generation and delivery, and is inconsistent with
the FPA 202(c) requirement of just and reasonable rates. 9

        2. The Commission erred by declining to require MISO to initiate a stakeholder process
to ensure that ratepayers subject to the order have a forum to address cost allocation and to ensure
that rates are just and reasonable.

           B. Argument

           1. The Commission erred in accepting the proposed cost-allocation method because
              it is not supported by substantial evidence in the record, ignores the obligations of
              NIPSCO’s existing and potential customers to pay NIPSCO rates for generation
              and delivery, and is inconsistent with the FPA 202(c) requirement of just and
              reasonable rates.

           In the Commission’s March 19 Order, the Commission granted NIPSCO’s proposed tariff,

which spreads costs across MISO’s north/central region without determining the reliability benefit

for those ratepayers. The March 19 Order, like the DOE Order, is not supported by substantial

evidence in the record. It fails to identify any reliability benefit that may be realized by customers

outside the NIPSCO territory associated with the Impacted Schahfer Units and does not address

how NIPSCO’s status as a vertically integrated utility may affect cost allocation. Specifically, in

allocating costs, the Commission should consider more than load ratio within MISO’s North and

Central region.

           There has been little to no opportunity for parties to assess the load ratio cost-allocation

mechanism adopted by the Commission as it relates to the Impacted Schahfer Units. The cost

allocation method should expressly consider whether either existing NIPSCO load or new, large



9
    16 U.S.C § 824d(a).

                                                    3
 load customers within the NIPSCO service area are utilizing the Impacted Schahfer Units. The

costs to keep Schahfer operating should be allocated to those who benefit from the plant, assuming

any benefit exists (which the IL OAG does not concede). Allocating those costs based on load

ratio without regard to any actual benefits provided by the Impacted Schahfer Units is unfair,

unjust, and unreasonable.

         In its Order at paragraph 4, the Commission stated:

         In the DOE Order, the Secretary of Energy determined that “an emergency exists in
         portions of the Midwest region of the United States due to a shortage of electric energy, a
         shortage of facilities for the generation of electric energy, and other causes.” Further, the
         Secretary of Energy determined that issuance of the DOE Order will “meet the emergency
         and serve the public interest.” Therefore, the Secretary of Energy directed MISO and
         NIPSCO to take all measures necessary to ensure that the Schahfer Units were available to
         operate and directed NIPSCO to keep the Schahfer Units open for 90 days, i.e., until March
         23, 2026. 10

         While the DOE order fails to identify the reliability benefits it claims, in allocating costs

the Commission should not perpetuate this error. Further, it is inconsistent with the FPA 202(c)

requirement of just and reasonable rates. 11 FERC must ensure that cost recovery and cost allocation

are just and reasonable, particularly when there are ratepayers who are not benefiting from, nor

causing, the costs.

         While the DOE Order does not reference the growth of large load customers who use more

than 50 megawatts of power, and that are responsible for much of the load growth in MISO as well

as in other regions like PJM, 12 the Commission should not adopt a cost allocation methodology

that ignores that large load customers may operate in the NIPSCO territory and take advantage of

Schahfer. Customers who may benefit (under the assumption that there are any benefits at all,


10
   March 19 Order at para. 4 (citing DOE Order at 1, Id., DOE Order at ordering para. (A), and DOE Order at 5) (
citations omitted).
11
   16 U.S.C § 824d(a).
12
   See, e.g., Catherine Boudreau, Indiana is getting $15 billion in Big Tech investment. Residents don't want to foot
the     energy     bill,  https://www.businessinsider.com/indiana-big-techs-ai-data-centers-energy-amazon-google-
microsoft-2025-2 (accessed April 20, 2026).

                                                         4
 which the IL OAG does not concede), including large load customers, should not be subsidized by

the rest of MISO North and Central customers by requiring MISO customers to cover the costs of

keeping the Impacted Schahfer Units operating based on load ratio.

         Certain large load data center companies even signed a ratepayer protection pledge to

protect ratepayers from subsidizing their costs, pledging that these large loads will build, bring, or

buy their generation. 13 Thus, the Commission should consider whether the Impacted Schahfer

Units are being retained to serve large load. Only customers who directly benefit (if there are any

benefits, which the IL OAG does not concede) from the Impacted Schahfer Units, which could

include these new loads, should be allocated those costs.

         The FPA 202(c) requirement of just and reasonable rates encompasses the principle of cost-

causation, or that ratepayers who supposedly benefit from the Impacted Schahfer Units should pay

the costs to keep the Impacted Schahfer Units operating. 14 Consistent with what multiple parties

have argued in this proceeding, the cost-causation principle requires that “in order to ensure just

and reasonable rates, FERC must make some reasonable effort to match costs to benefits.” 15 The

Commission should grant rehearing in order to address this principle.




13
        Ratepayer         Protection         Pledge,        The       White        House       (March     4,      2026),
https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/03/ratepayer-protection-pledge/.
14
   16 U.S.C § 824d(a); Illinois Com. Comm'n v. FERC, 576 F.3d 470, 476 (7th Cir. 2009) (“FERC is not authorized
to approve a pricing scheme that requires a group of utilities to pay for facilities from which its members derive no
benefits, or benefits that are trivial in relation to the costs sought to be shifted to its members.”)
15
   Old Dominion Elec. Coop. v. FERC, 898 F.3d 1254, 1263 (D.C. Cir. 2018). See also El Paso Elec. Co. v. FERC,
76 F.4th 352, 356 (5th Cir. 2023) (“The FPA requires that all rates and charges made, demanded, or received by any
public utility for or in connection with the transmission or sale of electric energy be just and reasonable. 16 U.S.C.S.
§ 824d(a). For decades, the FERC and the courts have understood this requirement to incorporate a cost-causation
principle.”); Long Island Power Auth. & Long Island Lighting Co. v. FERC, 27 F.4th 705, 709 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (citing
Midwest ISO Transmission Owners v. FERC, 373 F.3d 1361, 1368 (D.C. Cir. 2004)) (cleaned up) (“To be just and
reasonable, rates must ‘reflect to some degree the costs actually caused by the customer who must pay for them.’ This
‘cost-causation principle’ requires ‘comparing the costs assessed against a party to the burdens imposed or benefits
drawn by that party.’”).

                                                           5
        2. The Commission erred by declining to require MISO to initiate a stakeholder
          process to ensure that ratepayers subject to the order have a forum to address cost
          allocation and to ensure that rates are just and reasonable.

       There are various stakeholders in MISO. Unlike Indiana and many other MISO states,

Illinois is one of the few regions that is not vertically integrated. In effect, this tariff is shifting

costs that are generally part of an integrated utility’s rates onto residents in other states that are

covered by MISO without regard to the needs of either Indiana or each state. The DOE Order does

not identify the reliability benefit associated with keeping the Impacted Schahfer Units operating

and only makes general statements about reliability in MISO North and Central regions. In light

of this lack of specificity, it is critical that any cost allocation method adopted by the Commission

incorporate the opportunity to develop more detailed assessments of the benefits, if any, of keeping

the Impacted Schahfer Units open for various MISO regions and customers, including in Indiana.

       FERC should order the stakeholder process to provide the opportunity for stakeholders to

assess costs and any benefits to ensure that the charges associated with the plant and cost allocation

are based on the principle of cost causation where the cost causers are the cost payers. FERC must

ensure that cost recovery and cost allocation are just and reasonable, particularly when there are

ratepayers who are not benefitting from, nor causing, the costs.

III.   CONCLUSION

       WHEREFORE, for the foregoing reasons, the Office of the Illinois Attorney General

respectfully requests that the Commission grant rehearing.
